implementation_notes: Go has no classes or static members, so the registry is a package-level map plus an exported accessor; find-or-create holds sync.Mutex (or an RWMutex with a re-checked upgrade) across the lookup and the insert, because Go maps are not safe for concurrent use. Instances are pointers to a struct whose fields stay unexported, so the accessor is the only way in; sync.Once is not enough here - it makes initialisation once per program, not once per key.
pitfalls: A read-lock lookup followed by a write-lock insert must re-check the key after the upgrade (double-checked locking), or two goroutines can both create an instance.
Exporting the map, or an exported Register function, reopens the pattern: keep the map unexported and expose only the accessor.
A plain map written concurrently panics (fatal error: concurrent map writes); the registry is neither sync.Map nor safe by default.

variants.name: sync.Map.LoadOrStore registry
variants.idiom_name: sync.Map with LoadOrStore (keys written once, read many times)
variants.implementation_notes: When each key is written once and then read heavily - the registry's normal shape - sync.Map with LoadOrStore(key, newConn(key)) gives amortised-constant access without a hand-held mutex: LoadOrStore stores the given value only if the key is absent and returns the winner. The price is interface{} boxing, type assertions at every call site and the package's own warning that Map is specialised, so write-heavy or iteration-heavy shapes should stay on the mutex-guarded map.
pitfalls: LoadOrStore always evaluates its argument, so a racing caller builds a throwaway value - a real cost when construction opens a connection or allocates a buffer.
sync.Map has no len and no consistent snapshot; any shutdown path that must close or count instances needs Range or a companion mutex.
Type assertions at every call site move errors from compile time to run time; a generic mutex-guarded map is often clearer and no slower.
